0-20 clients:

This is the phase where you learn the business inside and out because you literally have no choice. You are the business.

20-50 clients:

This is where everything almost broke.

I was still doing fulfillment and managing all the client strategy myself and it wasn't sustainable. So I made the hardest shift: I gave up fulfillment.

Brought on a Director of Ops to take the lead on client work execution.

A big shift was starting hiring people who actually had experience instead of just whoever I could

List fatigue isn’t really a thing.

The idea is that if you email too much, people get bored, stop opening and unsubscribe.

What we actually see is closer to the opposite.

Sending too little, or sending inconsistently, does far more damage.

The worst pattern?

→ Send a bunch of emails one week
→ Go quiet for a couple of weeks
→ Come back hard for a sale

That hurts list health, engagement and unsubs more than sending 5-6 emails every week.

I’m not saying send 5-6 a week.

3-4 is usually the sweet spot.

But whatever you pick, stay consistent. #klaviyo

Most people think subject lines drive open rates.

They don’t.

Run a subject line A/B test, get a “”winner””, then run the exact same test a few months later.

It’s a coin flip whether the result holds.

That basically makes it meaningless.

Our only rules for subject lines:

✅ Sound like a human, not a corporation
✅ If you do A/B test them, pick the winner on sales, not opens

Stop overthinking your subject lines.  #klaviyo

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well

10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them

- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer
